title: Making Things Move: DIY Mechanisms for Inventors, Hobbyists, and Artists
creator: Dustyn Roberts; McGraw Hill
prerequisites: Basic measurement, force and torque; willingness to make small physical experiments.
access: Paid print or ebook; library availability varies.
why: A project-oriented bridge from static objects to moving mechanisms, with accessible explanations suited to makers before a formal machine-design text.
first_task: Choose one mechanism and redraw its load path, support points, motion range and possible pinch points for a small sensor mount.
limitations: Published in 2010; component and software examples need current checks. Reading does not qualify a mechanism for a particular load.
evidence_note: Publisher page confirms author, edition, publication date and an approach based on explanations, examples and DIY moving-mechanism projects. Recommendation is based on that description, not personal completion.

title: Choosing your motor, power supply, and Jrk
creator: Pololu
prerequisites: Voltage, current, power, torque and speed.
why: Connects motor behavior with the current and voltage demands that commonly surprise first-time mechanism builders.
first_task: For a candidate motor, distinguish free-run current, stall current and your driver's continuous and brief limits in a comparison table.
limitations: Written for one controller family. Apply the selection reasoning but use the actual motor and driver specifications; do not generalize operating tricks to unknown hardware.
evidence_note: Official guide explains voltage compatibility, free-running versus stall current, starting and reversal current, power-supply capability and controller current limits.

title: All About Stepper Motors
creator: Bill Earl; Adafruit Learning System
prerequisites: Basic DC circuits and the difference between torque and speed.
access: Free guide; hardware purchases are optional for reading.
why: Explains the appeal and practical limits of stepper positioning before the reader treats counted steps as guaranteed motion.
first_task: Read the introduction and driver-matching section; write why holding torque alone cannot select a motor for your desired operating speed.
limitations: Product examples are vendor-specific and some are older. Confirm current ratings, wiring and driver availability against actual datasheets.
evidence_note: Official guide identifies the author and includes sections on stepper operation, types, driving, matching the driver and frequently asked questions.

title: 6.002 Circuits and Electronics, Spring 2007
creator: Anant Agarwal; MIT OpenCourseWare
level: University introductory; intermediate after this handbook's first circuits lab
prerequisites: Algebra and basic physics for the opening material; calculus and differential equations become useful in dynamic-circuit analysis.
access: Free archived course materials, including lectures and exercises; no live grading or completion credential from the archive.
why: Provides a structured conceptual and problem-solving foundation behind the handbook's small practical circuits.
first_task: Watch the introductory lecture and work a resistive-network problem without consulting its solution; explain current and voltage signs.
limitations: An archived university course, not a self-paced maker kit. Laboratory equipment and later mathematical demands exceed the beginner bench route.
evidence_note: MIT page identifies instructor and term, undergraduate level, topics spanning resistive networks through dynamic circuits, and lecture, assignment, laboratory and examination materials.

title: Multimeters
creator: Ladyada; Adafruit Learning System
prerequisites: Voltage and current; an unpowered circuit or the handbook's current-limited low-voltage bench setup for practice.
why: Separates the measurement modes that a beginner can easily confuse and supports deliberate probe placement.
first_task: Read voltage and resistance sections, then identify the correct sockets and mode on your meter using its own manual.
limitations: Older illustrated equipment may differ from your meter. This recommendation does not extend the handbook lab to mains or high-energy measurements.
evidence_note: Official guide contains separate continuity, resistance, voltage and current sections, with illustrated measurement instructions.

title: Practical Electronics for Inventors, Fourth Edition
creator: Paul Scherz and Simon Monk; McGraw Hill
prerequisites: Algebra and the willingness to work small circuit examples before building larger projects.
access: Paid print or ebook; library access may be available.
why: A broad desk reference for moving from resistor calculations into component selection, analog circuits and practical prototypes.
first_task: Use its resistor and measurement material to explain the loaded divider, then consult one unfamiliar component chapter as a reference.
limitations: Broad coverage is not a substitute for a sequenced lab course. The 2016 edition's platforms and component examples require current documentation checks.
evidence_note: Publisher verifies authors, fourth edition, publication date and coverage of passive parts, semiconductors, sensors, power, digital electronics, programmable logic and motors.

title: CircuitJS electronic circuit simulator
creator: Paul Falstad and CircuitJS contributors
prerequisites: Nodes, voltage, current and basic component symbols.
access: Free browser simulator; no purchased hardware needed for the handbook's examples.
why: Makes voltage and current behavior visible while allowing quick component changes before a bench experiment.
first_task: Draw the handbook's 3 V, two-10 kΩ divider, then add a 10 kΩ load and explain the changed midpoint voltage.
limitations: Component models and ideal wires omit many physical effects. Some author instructions retain older applet wording; simulation does not verify wiring or component ratings.
evidence_note: Author instructions describe component editing, voltage/current displays, scope views, circuit files, and included resistor and divider examples.

title: Precision Labs: Analog-to-Digital Converters
creator: Texas Instruments
prerequisites: Voltage dividers, capacitance, frequency and the distinction between resolution and accuracy.
access: Free on-demand manufacturer training videos and associated learning material.
why: Connects numerical conversion with the analog conditions needed for trustworthy measurements.
first_task: Watch the basic-operation lesson and the aliasing/anti-aliasing lesson; reproduce the handbook's 18 Hz sampled-at-20 Hz comparison.
limitations: Later amplifier and converter-driver lessons are substantially more advanced; evaluation-board experiments require additional equipment.
evidence_note: Official series page lists short videos, quizzes and exercises covering architecture, DC/AC specifications, aliasing, noise, reference inputs and ADC drive design.

title: MT-101: Decoupling Techniques
creator: Analog Devices
prerequisites: Capacitance, frequency, supply current and a first schematic or PCB layout.
why: Explains why the physical path to a capacitor matters, supporting the move from a schematic to real power wiring.
first_task: Identify the supply-current loop through a chip's local capacitor and mark which connections should be physically short.
limitations: Examples concern analog and mixed-signal devices. Values and network choices must follow the actual chip and regulator requirements.
evidence_note: Official tutorial discusses supply sensitivity, local charge reservoirs, capacitor placement and inductance, with diagrams and example measurements.

title: MicroPython v1.26.0 RP2 quick reference
creator: MicroPython project
prerequisites: Python functions and conditionals; GPIO voltage limits and a correctly identified RP2-family board.
access: Free documentation and firmware; physical board optional for the desktop lab.
why: Provides the authoritative API counterpart to the handbook's button and timing model.
first_task: Read GPIO and the linked time API, then explain why the supplied hardware adaptation uses ticks_diff instead of raw tick subtraction.
limitations: Version-pinned for reproducibility rather than a claim to be newest. Board variants differ; APIs documented for another release may not match installed firmware.
evidence_note: Official released-version documentation covers the RP2 port, USB REPL, GPIO, UART, SPI, I²C, ADC and other peripherals; it distinguishes itself from development documentation.

title: Pico microcontroller boards
creator: Raspberry Pi
access: Free official board documentation and linked hardware references.
why: Helps prevent the common mistake of treating different board variants, chip names and physical pin numbers as interchangeable.
first_task: Identify your exact board and mark GP15, GND and the onboard indicator connection on its official pinout before wiring the optional button lab.
limitations: A hardware reference rather than a complete embedded-programming course. The supplied lab specifically targets the original non-wireless Pico/Pico H.
evidence_note: Official page distinguishes board generations and variants, explains microcontroller programming versus Linux systems, and links model-specific information.

title: Making Embedded Systems, Second Edition
creator: Elecia White; O'Reilly
prerequisites: Comfortable programming, preferably some C; basic circuits and one small microcontroller project.
access: Paid book or O'Reilly access; available preview material does not constitute full access.
why: A next step from making a board blink to organizing its behavior, diagnosing failures and working within hardware constraints.
first_task: Read the introductory architecture material and draw the tasks, data flow and failure boundaries of the sensor logger.
limitations: Not a first-language course or a board-specific wiring manual. Translate examples to your actual hardware rather than assuming identical peripherals.
evidence_note: Publisher identifies the author, second edition and embedded-system content, with preview and table-of-contents access. Assessment is based on those materials.

title: Getting Started in KiCad 10.0
creator: KiCad project
prerequisites: Ability to explain a simple circuit and identify its components and nodes.
access: Free official guide and open-source desktop software.
why: A coherent official workflow from schematic through physical layout and manufacturing outputs, matching the paper-first divider project.
first_task: Complete the introductory workflow, then capture the handbook's divider and perform a full-size paper footprint check before ordering anything.
limitations: Interface details vary by installed version. ERC and DRC do not validate circuit function, electrical safety or real component fit.
evidence_note: Official versioned guide covers schematic capture, annotation, footprints, ERC, board setup, routing, zones, DRC, 3D inspection and fabrication outputs.

title: AN11158: Understanding power MOSFET data sheet parameters
creator: Nexperia
prerequisites: Voltage, current, power and the basic role of a transistor as a controlled switch.
why: Teaches readers to interpret test conditions and limits instead of selecting a transistor from one attractive headline number.
first_task: Locate threshold voltage and on-resistance in a candidate device's datasheet; write down the different test conditions beside each.
limitations: Power-device analysis quickly becomes advanced. It is not a complete gate-driver design or permission to operate at absolute maximum ratings.
evidence_note: Official application note explains datasheet sections, electrical and thermal parameters, measurement conditions and safe operating area using a manufacturer device example.

title: Nand to Tetris
creator: Noam Nisan and Shimon Schocken
prerequisites: Boolean logic for the opening projects; programming becomes necessary for the later software stack.
access: Free self-study lecture/project materials under the site's stated terms; book and Coursera credential path are separate paid options.
why: Builds a concrete connection from a small truth table to a complete simulated computer rather than presenting logic gates as isolated symbols.
first_task: Complete the first gate project and test every input combination; explain why tying NAND inputs together produces inversion.
limitations: Works at a digital abstraction level, not transistor fabrication or PCB signal integrity. Check licensing terms for uses beyond personal/nonprofit study.
evidence_note: Official authors' site provides lectures, project materials and tools, describes free nonprofit self-study access, and distinguishes the paid Coursera certificate route.

title: Tiny Tapeout learning materials
creator: Tiny Tapeout
prerequisites: Logic gates and truth tables; HDL and testing skills for more substantial digital submissions.
access: Online learning and design guidance are available; physical chip submission, hardware and workshops have separate program-dependent requirements and costs.
why: Makes the path from simulated logic to manufactured silicon visible while providing smaller learning exercises before any fabrication commitment.
first_task: Use the logic-gate exercises and semiconductor introduction to distinguish a simulated gate, transistor layout and a manufactured chip.
limitations: Not a replacement for a semiconductor or VLSI curriculum. Manufacturing schedules, process choices and submission conditions must be checked when planning a real chip.
evidence_note: Official site lists digital design and truth-table lessons, SiliWiz semiconductor exercises, HDL testing resources, workshops and silicon-submission paths.
